baseProblem.statement: Given a sorted array that has been rotated at some unknown pivot, find the index of a target value in O(log n) time. Return -1 if not found.

rounds.question: Standard binary search needs a fully sorted array. What property of a rotated sorted array preserves enough order for binary search to still work?
options: Every element is still smaller than every element after it
At least one half of any split around the midpoint is fully sorted
The pivot is always at a predictable index
The array can be re-sorted in O(log n) time
rounds.explanation: Cut the array anywhere; one side is always normally sorted. That's the half where you can check 'is target in this range' in O(1).

rounds.question: At each step, how do you decide which half to recurse into?
options: Compare target to mid; if smaller, go left; if larger, go right
Identify which half is sorted, check if target falls in its range, recurse accordingly
Always go right unless mid equals target
Recurse into both halves and combine results
rounds.explanation: You can't compare to mid alone because the rotation breaks the ordering assumption. Identifying the sorted half first restores reliable range checks.

rounds.question: What's the time complexity of the optimal solution?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
rounds.explanation: Each step halves the search space, just like standard binary search. The rotation adds bookkeeping but doesn't change the depth.

rounds.question: What if the array contains duplicates? How does the algorithm change?
options: It still runs in O(log n) — duplicates don't affect the logic
It degrades to O(n) in the worst case because you can't always tell which half is sorted
It returns immediately as soon as any duplicate is found
Duplicates make the problem unsolvable
rounds.explanation: If nums[left] == nums[mid] == nums[right], you can't determine which side is sorted and must scan linearly past the duplicates. Standard interview follow-up question.

rounds.question: Which input is most likely to expose a bug in the half-identification logic?
options: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], target = 3 (unrotated)
[3, 1], target = 1 (minimum rotation)
[5, 1, 2, 3, 4], target = 5 (rotated by one)
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5], target = 6 (target not present)
rounds.explanation: With only two elements, off-by-one errors in identifying the sorted half show up immediately. Many implementations handle large rotated arrays but fail here.
